lesson.title: Why We Are the Way We Are: The Evolutionary Perspective on Behavior
lesson.summary: This section introduces the evolutionary perspective, the idea that many widespread human behavioral tendencies exist because they helped ancestors survive and reproduce, and explains both its explanatory power and its limits.
lesson.body:
The evolutionary perspective in psychology looks at behavior through a very different lens than the research designs covered so far. Rather than asking how much of an individual difference between two people comes from genes versus environment, it asks a broader species level question: why do humans in general tend to think, feel, and behave in certain characteristic ways at all. The evolutionary perspective proposes that many widespread psychological tendencies exist today because they helped our distant ancestors survive long enough to reproduce and raise offspring who also survived, generation after generation, across an enormous span of time.

This perspective builds directly on the heredity and behavior concepts covered earlier in this section. If a behavioral tendency has no genetic basis at all and is purely learned individually within a single lifetime, it cannot be shaped by the generational process the evolutionary perspective describes. Evolutionary explanations therefore tend to focus on broad predispositions that show up reliably across cultures, such as a general tendency toward caution around certain kinds of danger, rather than specific learned skills like knowing how to drive a car or speak a particular language, which clearly depend on nurture and individual experience rather than inherited tendency.

A commonly cited illustration involves fear responses. Many people across very different cultures show a fast, easily learned fear reaction to things like snakes or heights, even when they grew up somewhere those dangers were rarely encountered directly, and this fear tends to be acquired more readily than fear of comparably dangerous modern hazards like electrical outlets or fast moving cars. One explanation offered by the evolutionary perspective is that ancestors who were biologically primed to quickly learn caution around ancestrally dangerous things were more likely to survive and pass that predisposition along, while modern hazards have not been around nearly long enough, in evolutionary terms, for a similar predisposition to develop toward them.

Evolutionary explanations come with an important caution, and it connects back to the scientific method discussed at the very start of this section. Because psychologists cannot travel back and directly observe the ancestral environments in which these predispositions supposedly evolved, it is tempting to construct a plausible sounding evolutionary story after already knowing the outcome, which is a much weaker form of evidence than a prediction made and tested in advance. The evolutionary perspective is most convincing, and most scientific, when it generates specific predictions that could in principle be shown to be false, rather than simply offering a tidy explanation after the fact for whatever behavior happens to already exist.

Understanding why the evolutionary perspective works the way it does requires understanding the actual mechanism that drives it: natural selection, the process covered in the next section.
